name: East Semitic
defining_innovation: The first Semitic languages to be written, Akkadian and Eblaite, in cuneiform borrowed from Sumerian. Akkadian lost most of the Semitic guttural consonants, which often left an e-vowel behind.

chapters.title: Akkadian
chapters.body:
Akkadian is the oldest attested Semitic language, and its written record spans more than 2,500 years. Semitic personal names appear in Sumerian texts around 2600 BCE, and with Sargon of Akkad (c. 2334 BCE) Akkadian became the language of an empire. It was written in cuneiform, the wedge-shaped script invented for Sumerian, an unrelated language. Akkadian speakers lived alongside Sumerian speakers for centuries, and Akkadian took from Sumerian both vocabulary and, unusually for Semitic, verb-final word order.

Akkadian later split into Babylonian in the south and Assyrian in the north, and it produced the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, the Code of Hammurabi and a vast archive of letters, contracts and scholarship. It also lost most of the guttural consonants that other Semitic languages keep, and they often left an *e* behind them.

chapters.title: Ebla, and the Long Fade
chapters.body:
In 1974–75 excavators at Tell Mardikh in Syria found the archives of Ebla, thousands of tablets from the 24th century BCE in a Semitic language now called Eblaite. Most scholars group it with Akkadian as East Semitic, though some see it as closer to West Semitic.

In the 2nd millennium BCE Akkadian was the diplomatic language of the Near East: pharaohs and Levantine kings wrote to each other in it in the Amarna letters. From the 8th century BCE Aramaic replaced it as the everyday language, first of the Assyrian empire and then of its successors. Akkadian survived as a language of scholarship. The last datable cuneiform tablets, astronomical texts from Babylon, come from the 1st century CE.

speakers.note: Akkadian was probably displaced as a spoken language by Aramaic during the 1st millennium BCE, though it was written until the 1st century CE.

sources.citation: Weninger, Stefan, ed. 2011. The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sample.translation: He who saw the Deep, the foundation of the land (opening line of the Epic of Gilgamesh)

sources.citation: George, Andrew R. 2003. The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic: Introduction, Critical Edition and Cuneiform Texts. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.date: Before and during the 3rd millennium BCE
turning_points.title: Loss of the gutturals
turning_points.description: Akkadian loses most Proto-Semitic laryngeal and pharyngeal consonants (`*ʔ *h *ḥ *ʕ *ġ`), often changing a neighbouring *a* to *e*: `*baʕal-` 'lord' → Akkadian *bēlu* (Hebrew *baʕal*). Contact with Sumerian, which lacked such sounds, is a frequently suggested cause.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John. 2011. A Grammar of Akkadian, 3rd ed. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.

turning_points.title: Akkadian in cuneiform
turning_points.description: Semitic names and then texts are written in Sumerian cuneiform, making Akkadian the earliest recorded Semitic language. Decipherment in the 19th century, driven by Henry Rawlinson's copying of the trilingual Behistun inscription, reopened this record.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John. 2011. A Grammar of Akkadian, 3rd ed. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.

turning_points.title: The Sumerian–Akkadian convergence
turning_points.description: Centuries of bilingualism in southern Mesopotamia give Akkadian verb-final word order and Sumerian vocabulary, while Sumerian takes Akkadian loans. Sumerian stopped being spoken early in the 2nd millennium BCE but lived on as a written language.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John. 2011. A Grammar of Akkadian, 3rd ed. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.

turning_points.title: The Ebla archives
turning_points.description: The royal archives of Ebla in Syria preserve thousands of cuneiform tablets in Eblaite. Its classification, as East Semitic with Akkadian or as something separate, is debated.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John & Aaron D. Rubin. 2011. Phyla and waves: Models of classification of the Semitic languages. In The Semitic Languages: An International Handbook, ed. Stefan Weninger. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

turning_points.title: Babylonian and Assyrian
turning_points.description: Akkadian divides into Babylonian in the south and Assyrian in the north, each with its own stages. Babylonian becomes the international language of diplomacy, used in the 14th-century BCE Amarna letters.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John. 2011. A Grammar of Akkadian, 3rd ed. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.

turning_points.title: Aramaic replaces Akkadian
turning_points.description: Aramaic becomes the spoken language of Mesopotamia, and Akkadian retreats into temple scholarship. When it stopped being spoken is uncertain. The last datable cuneiform texts are astronomical tablets from the 1st century CE.

sources.citation: Huehnergard, John. 2011. A Grammar of Akkadian, 3rd ed. Winona Lake: Eisenbrauns.
Gzella, Holger. 2015. A Cultural History of Aramaic. Leiden: Brill.
